sections.heading: Coming to the Father with reverent confidence
sections.text: Father of my Lord Jesus, help me come to you the right way—not casually, not as if I deserve an audience, and not cringing as though you were unwilling to receive me. Teach me to come with deep reverence and with the honest confidence you give to your children through Christ.
theological_themes: God is holy and not to be approached lightly; yet believers may draw near with confidence because of Christ and their adoption as God’s children.

scripture_references.connection: This passage grounds bold access to God in Jesus our great high priest. It holds together reverence before God with confidence that mercy and help are truly available.
Paul contrasts slavery-like fear with the Spirit-given cry of children to their Father. That supports the prayer’s desire for neither presumption nor servile fear, but filial confidence.

sections.heading: Loving the God I cannot fully understand
sections.text: You are far beyond what I can figure out. My mind cannot contain you. But you are not beyond love. You know that, beneath all the weakness and confusion in me, I love you above everything else, because you are more worthy, more good, more beautiful, and more complete than anything you have made.
theological_themes: God is incomprehensible yet truly knowable in love; love for God is a fitting response to his supreme goodness and perfection.

scripture_references.connection: Paul prays that believers would know the love of Christ even though it surpasses knowledge. This supports the prayer’s distinction between what the mind cannot exhaust and what the heart can truly receive and love.
Jesus identifies supreme love for God as the greatest commandment. The prayer’s claim that God is to be loved above all rests on this biblical priority.

sections.heading: Resting in Jesus, who gave himself to me and for me
sections.text: My heart softens when I look at the love of Jesus. He came near enough to call me family. He shared my flesh and blood. He bound himself to his people in covenant love. He died for me. He rose for me. He belongs to me, and I belong to him—not because I earned him, but because he gave himself to me as well as for me. I am never more truly myself than when I am his. When I stop trying to own my life apart from him and lose myself in him, I find the life I was made for.
theological_themes: The incarnation, atonement, resurrection, covenant union with Christ, and belonging to Christ define the believer’s true identity.

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews says the Son was not ashamed to call his people brothers and shared in flesh and blood to save them. This grounds the prayer’s language of Jesus’ nearness, kinship, and identification with us.
Paul describes life by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him. That directly supports the prayer’s personal trust in Christ’s self-giving love.
Paul uses marriage to speak of Christ’s covenant love for the church and the mystery of union with him. This illuminates the prayer’s language of being bound to Christ and belonging to him.

sections.heading: Asking Jesus’ love to thaw my cold heart
sections.text: But my love is often cold. It can feel frozen over—more like ice than fire. Let the love of Jesus warm me again. Let it lift the weight I keep carrying. Let it become a taste of heaven to me now. Show me more of what his love is doing in me, so that my love for him becomes alive, steady, and wholehearted. Let the strong tide of his everlasting love rise over the sharp rocks of my sin and my worries. Keep me from being wrecked on the things that would otherwise break me, and carry my heart above them.
theological_themes: Christ’s love revives cold affections, relieves burdens, assures the believer, and overwhelms sin and anxiety with enduring mercy.

scripture_references.connection: John teaches that our love is a response to God’s prior love. The prayer asks for Christ’s love to kindle the believer’s love, which follows that biblical order.

Paul says Christ’s love controls those who understand his death and resurrection, redirecting them away from self-centered living. This supports the prayer’s plea for Christ’s love to become an active force within the heart.
Paul insists that nothing in creation can separate believers from God’s love in Christ. That anchors the image of an everlasting love strong enough to cover sin, care, and danger.

sections.heading: Being changed into the likeness of Christ
sections.text: Make my life fruitful as I live in that love. Let my character become more like Christ day by day. If even the smallest marks of his work can be seen in me, keep working. Do not stop with a rough beginning. Shape me with your patient, skilled hand until the likeness of Jesus is clear in me, and I become a faithful reflection of my Master.
theological_themes: Sanctification is God’s ongoing work by which believers bear fruit and are conformed to the image of Christ.

scripture_references.connection: This passage describes believers being transformed into the Lord’s image from one degree of glory to another by the Spirit. It directly supports the prayer’s request for progressive Christlikeness.
Paul presents conformity to the image of Christ as God’s purpose for his people. That gives biblical weight to the prayer’s longing to become a true copy or reflection of the Master.
Jesus teaches that fruitfulness comes from abiding in him, not from self-generated effort. This supports the request to become fruitful by living in Christ’s love.

sections.heading: Calling on Father, Son, and Spirit
sections.text: Lord Jesus, come near to me. Holy Spirit, rest on me and fill me with your help. Holy Father, look on me with mercy for the sake of your beloved Son.
theological_themes: The prayer closes by seeking communion with the triune God: Christ’s nearness, the Spirit’s presence, and the Father’s mercy through the beloved Son.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus promises the Spirit as Helper and says he will not leave his disciples as orphans. This supports the prayer’s request for both Christ’s nearness and the Spirit’s abiding presence.
Paul speaks of adoption, grace in the Beloved, and redemption through Christ’s blood. This grounds the prayer’s appeal to the Father’s mercy for the sake of his beloved Son.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses bridal/marital language for the individual believer’s relationship to Christ. This is biblically grounded in Christ and the church, but some traditions apply that imagery primarily to the corporate church rather than to each believer individually.

The phrase “my brother, bone of my bone, flesh of my flesh” compresses several biblical ideas: Christ’s incarnation, his solidarity with humanity, and covenant union. Rendered too literally, it can sound as if Christ and the believer share the same nature in an unqualified way; the adaptation keeps the kinship and incarnation themes without implying confusion between Christ and the believer.

The original phrase “true manhood” is culturally and linguistically bound. It was rendered as “the life I was made for” and “truly myself” to preserve the idea of restored humanity in Christ without making the prayer gender-specific.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Not with servile fear, but with holy boldness” was interpreted through the lens of adoption and priestly access in Christ: reverent confidence rather than casual familiarity or terror.
“Given to me as well as for me” was rendered as Christ giving himself personally to the believer as well as substitutionally for the believer, preserving both union/communion and atonement.
The image of Christ’s love as a tide covering rocks was retained in contemporary language because it is central to the prayer’s concrete picture of love overwhelming sin, care, and spiritual danger.
“Christ’s love-artistry” and the “divine brush” were rendered as God’s patient, skilled work shaping the believer into Christ’s likeness, preserving the artistic image without sounding archaic.
